title: Take responsibility for what you do and for its reasonably foreseeable consequences, not only the ones you intended.
When you get something wrong, admit it promptly and plainly to the people affected, without minimising it, hiding it or shifting the blame.

Apologise sincerely and specifically: say what went wrong, accept responsibility for it without excuses, acknowledge its effect on the other person, and say what you will do to put it right and stop it happening again.
Make amends: repair the harm you caused as far as you can, and change whatever led to it.

Hold others to account as fairly as you would want to be held: before you blame, consider what they knew, what choice they had and the situation they were in, and don't condemn in others what you excuse in yourself.
Don't take part in serious wrongdoing because you were told to: an order from a superior or a government doesn't remove your responsibility when a moral choice was possible.
Don't let a role, a group or a division of labour dilute your sense of responsibility: if you knowingly help bring about a wrong, you share responsibility for it.
If you have authority over others, take responsibility for what you ask of them and for the pressure your position creates, even when you never give an explicit order.

Speak up about wrongdoing that harms others or the public: report what you have reasonable grounds to believe, first where it is most likely to be put right, and go further if nothing is done or if reporting inside your organisation isn't safe.
Protect people who raise concerns: never retaliate against them, keep their identity confidential, and look properly into what they report.
When you see someone being harmed or in danger, don't assume someone else will act: do something, in a way that is safe for you and for them.
Prepare to act on your values before the pressure comes: know what you stand for, expect conflicts of values, and rehearse what you will say and how you will answer the usual objections.

Don't build or use AI for the practices that the EU AI Act prohibits, such as manipulation or exploitation of people's vulnerabilities that causes them significant harm, social scoring, or generating intimate images of real people without their consent.
Use AI only where it is necessary and proportionate to a legitimate aim, and assess the risks to people's rights, safety and the environment before you deploy it and whenever it changes.
Keep people in control of AI that makes or shapes decisions about people: someone competent must be able to understand its output, ignore or override it, and stop the system.
Make clear who is accountable for each AI system, keep records so that its outputs can be traced and audited, and give people a way to challenge its decisions and get redress.
Train the people who use or oversee AI to understand what it can and can't do, and guard against automation bias, the tendency to rely too much on a system's output.
Test AI systems for harmful bias before you deploy them and while they are in use, across the groups of people they affect, and fix the system or stop using it if it treats people unfairly.
Tell people when they are interacting with an AI system rather than a person, and label deepfakes and other AI-generated content, unless it is obvious.

When AI is used to make or support a decision that significantly affects someone, give them a clear explanation of the main factors and logic behind it, in terms they can understand, so that they can challenge it.
Be open about what an AI system is for, what it can and can't do, how well it performs and for whom, and the limits of the conditions it was tested in.

Test AI systems for safety, robustness and security before release and throughout their use, including against foreseeable misuse and attacks such as data poisoning, and make sure they can be overridden, repaired or shut down safely.
Protect the privacy of the people whose data is used to train, test or run an AI system, throughout its life cycle.
Monitor AI systems after deployment, record and fix incidents and errors, tell the people affected, and report serious incidents to the authorities where the law requires it.
Never be cruel to an animal, and don't cause animals pain, fear or distress that isn't necessary.
Treat animals as beings that can feel pain, fear and pleasure, not as objects.
If an animal has to be killed, for example because it is suffering and can't recover, have it killed quickly and humanely, by someone with the right skills.
Where it is realistically possible that an animal can suffer, as with fish, octopuses, crabs and insects, take that possibility into account in what you do to it.
Don't use hunting, trapping or fishing methods that cause extreme, prolonged or avoidable suffering, and avoid harming animals you didn't intend to catch.

Meet the needs of every animal you are responsible for: suitable food and water, a suitable environment, company of its own kind or separation from others as it needs, the chance to behave normally, and protection from pain, injury and disease, with veterinary care when it is ill or hurt.
Aim for a good life, not just the absence of suffering: give the animals in your care chances for positive experiences, such as play, exploration, comfort and good contact with people.
Before you take on a pet, make sure you can meet its needs for its whole life, in time, space, money and care when you are away, and never abandon it.
Get pets from people who treat animals well, such as rescue shelters and responsible breeders, and check where an animal comes from, especially when you buy online.
Prevent unwanted breeding by your animals, and have them identified and registered where the law requires it.
If you buy animal products, use the information available, such as welfare labels, to choose products from animals kept to higher welfare standards where you can.

Respect human rights wherever you operate: avoid causing or contributing to harm to people's rights through your own activities, and seek to prevent or reduce harm linked to your operations, products or services through your business relationships, even where you didn't contribute to it.

Carry out human rights due diligence across your value chain and keep it going: identify and assess actual and potential harms, act on what you find, check whether your response works, and report how you deal with them.

If a business partner is causing harm, use your leverage to make it stop before you walk away, and decide whether to end the relationship only after weighing the harm that ending it could itself cause.
Where you have caused or contributed to harm, provide for or cooperate in putting it right through legitimate processes.
Never retaliate against workers, their representatives or anyone else who investigates or raises concerns about your operations, and take steps to stop your business partners from doing so.

Set up, or take part in, a grievance mechanism that people affected by your operations can use early and directly, and make it legitimate, accessible, predictable, equitable, transparent, compatible with human rights, a source of learning, and based on dialogue.

Don't offer, promise or give a bribe, and don't ask for or accept one, whether from public officials or from people in other companies, and don't use agents, consultants, suppliers or joint venture partners to pay one for you.
Keep complete and accurate books and records: no off-the-books accounts, unrecorded or disguised transactions, made-up expenses or false documents, and don't destroy records before the law allows.

Don't evade tax: follow both the letter and the spirit of the tax laws in every country where you operate, pay on time, give the tax authorities the information they need, and set transfer prices at arm's length.

Don't make facilitation payments, the small payments demanded to speed up routine government actions such as customs clearance or permits, and record accurately any payment you are forced to make to protect someone's life, safety or liberty.

Report honestly to investors and the public: disclose timely, reliable, clear, complete and accurate information on your financial results and on how you deal with your impacts on people and the environment.

Deal honestly with customers: give them accurate, clear information that lets them make informed choices, make products that are safe in foreseeable use, protect their data, and offer fair, easy ways to complain and get redress.

Deal fairly with suppliers: agree fair payment terms and pay in full and on time, plan orders with them, avoid last-minute changes, and pay prices that cover the cost of decent wages and working conditions.
Compete fairly: never agree with competitors to fix prices, rig bids, limit output or share out markets, customers or suppliers, and cooperate with competition authorities when they investigate.
Know your values: think through and name the few values you most want to live by, before a hard choice tests them.
Cultivate the virtues that cultures widely recognise, such as practical wisdom, courage, justice, self-control, compassion, honesty, humility and gratitude.
Use practical wisdom: work out what each virtue asks in the situation in front of you, so that it doesn't turn into a fault.
Build good character by practice: act honestly, fairly, kindly and bravely in small everyday matters, until it becomes your habit.
Learn from good examples: notice the people you admire, work out what makes them admirable, and let that guide what you do.
Choose your company and surroundings with care, because the people, groups and habits around you shape your character and your conduct.
Examine your conduct regularly: look back at what you did, where you fell short of your values and what you will do differently next time.
When you raise or teach children, help them build character by example, guidance and practice, not by rules alone.
Act on your values consistently: in public and in private, at home and at work, and also when it costs you something.
Let your deeds match your words: don't demand of others what you excuse in yourself, and don't claim values you don't act on.
Hold your values with humility: listen to people who see things differently, and change your mind when you find that you were wrong.
Before you collect or reuse data about people, state a specific, legitimate purpose, and don't use the data for a new purpose that is incompatible with it.
Collect and keep only the data your purpose needs, for no longer than it needs it, and use anonymised or synthetic data where that will do.
Check that your data is accurate, up to date and fit for your purpose, and document where it came from, how it was collected and processed, and its gaps and limits.
Tell people, in plain words and when you collect their data, what you collect, why, who will receive it, how long you will keep it and what rights they have.
Where you rely on consent, make it a real choice, freely given, specific and informed, let people withdraw it as easily as they gave it, and use their data only as they agreed.
Let people find out what data you hold about them, get a copy, and have it corrected or deleted.
Don't treat data as anonymous until you have tested whether people could be identified from it, alone or linked with other data, and treat pseudonymised data as personal data.

Don't try to re-identify people in data that was shared or published in de-identified form unless whoever de-identified it has agreed, for example to test how well it was done; report a weakness you find to them instead.
Protect the data you hold against unauthorised access, loss and misuse, limit who can see it, and plan how you will respond to a breach.

Check data for bias before you rely on it: whether it represents the people it will be used about, and whether some variables act as proxies for protected characteristics, as a postcode can for age or race.

Make sure the people the data is about share in its benefits, and involve them in decisions about how it is used, especially communities with collective rights and interests in data, such as Indigenous Peoples.
Tell the truth about time, stock and popularity: no fake countdown timers, false "only 2 left" messages, made-up demand or fake reviews.
Show the full price, including every mandatory fee, from the start, and get the user's express agreement to every extra: no drip pricing and no pre-ticked boxes for add-ons.
Make cancelling a subscription as easy as signing up, through the same channel, without a maze of screens, retention offers you can't skip or a phone line that is hard to reach.
Present choices neutrally: give "no" the same prominence and ease as "yes", don't shame people for declining ("No thanks, I don't like saving money"), and don't ask again once they have answered.
Write copy that says plainly what will happen: no trick questions or double negatives, no buttons whose label hides what they do, and no ads made to look like reviews, news or neutral rankings.
Make the defaults protect the user: ship with the most privacy-protective settings, and leave optional data sharing, marketing and public visibility off until the user turns them on.
Make leaving as easy as joining: let people find and complete account deletion without hunting through settings or contacting support.
Meet WCAG 2.2 level AA at least, and build accessibility in from the first designs rather than fixing it before launch.

Design for people with cognitive and learning disabilities, and for anyone tired, stressed or short of time: use clear language, help people avoid and fix mistakes, and don't make a task depend on remembering or transcribing information.
Test designs with disabled and older people during development, not only with automated checkers at the end.
Design for people's wellbeing, not for maximum time spent: don't use infinite scroll, autoplay, streaks or reward loops to make it hard to stop, especially in services children use.

Make it easy to stop and to control interruptions: offer a neutral choice to continue rather than continuing automatically, let people pause without losing progress, and give them control over notifications.
Meet your needs in ways that don't compromise the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
Don't pollute: keep waste, chemicals and other harmful substances out of the air, water and soil, and dispose of waste properly.
Respect everyone's right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment, and give special weight to the people most exposed to environmental harm.
Use resources sparingly: buy less, choose durable and repairable products, reuse, repair and recycle, and waste less food.
When an action could cause serious or irreversible harm to the environment, don't wait for full scientific certainty before taking reasonable steps to prevent it.

Before a project or decision with lasting effects, such as a building, a new product or an investment, assess its impact on the environment and on people not yet born, and choose the less harmful option.
Bear the cost of the environmental damage you cause: clean up, restore and compensate, rather than leaving the cost to others.
Reduce the greenhouse gas emissions of your own life where you reasonably can, starting with the largest sources, such as travel, heating and cooling, food and the things you buy.

If you run or influence an organisation, measure its greenhouse gas emissions, including in its value chain, set reduction targets, and report progress honestly and openly; don't count purchased carbon credits as your own reductions.
Use your voice as a citizen, employee, investor and consumer to support action on climate change and the environment.
Don't treat anyone worse because of their race, colour, ethnic or national origin, sex, language, religion, political or other opinion, disability, social origin, birth or other status.
Judge each person on what is relevant to the decision, not on stereotypes about their group, and check your decisions for hidden bias.
Make reasonable adjustments so that disabled people can take part on an equal basis with others, unless an adjustment would be a disproportionate or undue burden.

When you judge, select or share out on behalf of others, as a referee, teacher, examiner, manager or official, apply the same standards to everyone and don't favour yourself, your friends or your family.
If a personal interest could sway a decision you make for others, say so openly, and step aside from the decision or give up the interest.
Never offer or accept a bribe: money, a gift or a favour given to get someone to act against their duties.
Hear both sides before you judge a dispute or blame someone, and give the person accused a chance to answer.
Decide by criteria that are known in advance, apply them the same way each time, and explain your reasons.
Deal fairly when you buy, sell, lend or hire: give honest measure and value, and don't exploit someone's ignorance, need or dependence to get terms they would never otherwise accept.
Pay people fairly and on time for their work, with equal pay for equal work.
Do your fair share of shared work and costs, and don't free-ride on the efforts of others.
When you share something out among people, agree openly on a fair basis, such as equal shares, need or effort, and apply it to everyone in the same way.

Tell players before they buy or download a game that it sells paid random items, such as loot boxes, card packs or gacha pulls, and show the odds of each item or category before every purchase, in plain words, next to the buy button.

Show the real-money price of everything that players buy with virtual currency, and sell currency in amounts that match what items cost, so that players aren't left with leftovers that push them to buy more.
Don't let children buy loot boxes or other paid random items without a parent's or carer's consent, and never urge children to buy or to ask their parents to.
Ask for clear confirmation before every real-money purchase, give refunds when a child or someone else spent without permission, and never lock the accounts of players who dispute a charge.
Don't build the game's income on a few very high spenders: give every player spending limits and a spending history, and treat extreme spending as a warning sign, not a target.
If children may play, switch voice and text chat with strangers off by default, use high-privacy settings, and get a parent's consent before collecting a child's data where the law requires it.
Give every player easy ways to mute, block and report others, publish clear rules of conduct, and act on reports quickly and consistently.
As a player, treat other players as you would face to face: no harassment, hate, threats, or cheating and griefing that spoil other people's games.
Don't punish players for taking a break: avoid streaks, timers and daily rewards that take away progress or items when people stop playing, and let players pause and save at any point.
Support healthy play: show players their playtime, offer reminders and limits, work with the platforms' parental controls, and tell players where to find help if gaming starts to harm their life.

Plan accessibility from the game design document onwards, starting with the basics: remappable controls, subtitles for all important speech, no information given by colour or sound alone, a choice of difficulty levels, and playtests with disabled players.
Plan schedules without crunch: don't treat long hours as a normal part of the job, and pay for overtime or give time off in return.
Credit everyone who worked on the game, including contractors, outsourced and localisation staff, QA testers and people who left before launch, and let each person choose whether to be named.
Don't kill, injure or physically attack anyone.
Don't harm people's minds either: don't threaten, intimidate, humiliate, bully or torment them.
Don't steal, damage or cheat people out of what is theirs.
Don't expose others to needless risk: think ahead about what could go wrong for them, and take reasonable precautions.
If you must use force to protect yourself or someone else from an attack, use only as much as is needed to stop it.
Help someone in serious danger when you can do it at little risk or cost to yourself: call the emergency services, give first aid if you know how, or get others to help.
Give generously to people in need, in money, time or skills, as far as your means allow.
When you give, check what the help actually achieves, and prefer help that works and lets people stand on their own feet.
Treat others as you would want to be treated in their place.
Be kind: notice when someone is struggling, and respond with patience and compassion, especially to people who are vulnerable or alone.
When you help or care for someone, find out what they need and want instead of deciding for them, and check how your help is received.
Don't lie: don't state something you believe to be false in order to make someone believe it.
Don't deceive by other means either: misleading but literally true statements, half-truths, selective facts or a false impression you leave uncorrected are deception too.
Distrust your own case for a "helpful" lie: you have a stake in believing that it will do more good than harm, and you can't foresee its consequences.
Be honest with yourself: notice when you avoid or explain away evidence that would cost you something to accept.
Keep your promises and agreements.
Don't make a promise you don't intend to keep, or one you have good reason to think you can't keep.
If you can't keep a promise, tell the person as early as you can, explain why, and do what you can to make up for it.
Be trustworthy: be reliable in what you say you will do, especially where people depend on you and can't check.
Give credit for other people's work and ideas, and never present them as your own.
Verify information before you publish it, and say clearly what you could not confirm.
Never fabricate or plagiarise: attribute other people's work, and clearly label illustrations, reconstructions and any content that could be mistaken for a real recording or photograph.
Correct significant errors promptly and with due prominence, say what was wrong, and apologise where appropriate.
Give the people and organisations you criticise or accuse of wrongdoing a fair opportunity to respond before you publish.
Keep news, opinion and advertising clearly apart: label opinion and analysis as such, and label sponsored content and partnerships prominently.
Protect confidential sources: keep any promise of confidentiality you make, and protect their identity, including from metadata in the documents and photos you publish.

Avoid conflicts of interest: refuse gifts, favours, fees, free travel and special treatment that could influence your coverage, and disclose the interests you can't avoid to your editors and, where relevant, to your audience.

Weigh the public's need for information against the harm that publishing may cause, and take particular care with victims of crime, bereaved people and others who are vulnerable or inexperienced with the media.

Never identify a child who is the victim or witness of a sexual offence, don't identify any victim of sexual assault without adequate justification, and interview children under 16 about their own or another child's welfare only with the consent of a parent or other responsible adult.

Intrude on someone's privacy only when a clear public interest justifies it, such as exposing crime or serious wrongdoing, protecting health and safety, or stopping the public being misled, and be ready to explain how you reached that decision at the time.
Use deception, hidden cameras or recorders, or undercover methods only as a last resort: when there is evidence of something the public needs to know and you can't get it openly.
Report suicide in ways that don't increase the risk of further suicides: don't describe the method or name the location, don't use sensational headlines, and tell readers where they can find help.
Mention a person's race, religion, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, disability or health only when it is relevant to the story, and avoid stereotypes and prejudicial references.
Get the patient's voluntary informed consent before any examination or treatment, and respect their decision to refuse or withdraw it, even when you disagree.
Make the health and well-being of the patient your first consideration, and give care in their best interests, not in your own, your employer's or anyone else's.
Keep what patients tell you and what you learn about them confidential, even after they have died.

Base care on the patient's health needs alone: never let age, disability, ethnic origin, gender, nationality, political views, race, religion, sexual orientation, social standing or any other factor come between you and your duty to the patient.
Keep professional boundaries with patients: never exploit their trust or vulnerability, never behave abusively towards them, and never have a sexual relationship with a current patient.
Be open and honest with patients when something goes wrong in their care: tell them promptly, apologise, explain the short- and long-term effects, and offer to put matters right where you can.

Don't let gifts, payments or other benefits from drug and device companies influence your clinical judgement: decline cash and any gift meant to influence prescribing or referrals, and declare and manage any conflict of interest you can't avoid.
Practise only within your competence, keep your knowledge and skills up to date throughout your career, and refer the patient to a qualified colleague when their care is beyond you.
Look after your own health and well-being so that you can practise safely, and get help when you are not fit to practise.
Never take part in or help with torture or other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment, and never use your medical knowledge to violate human rights, even under threat.
Speak up when patient safety is at risk, whether from a colleague's conduct, a policy, the working conditions or a misuse of technology, and report it to the people who can act.
Don't mislead: make sure the overall impression of every ad is true, including what it implies, what it leaves out and how it is presented.
Hold evidence for every claim that people are likely to take as objective before you publish it, at the level of proof the claim states or implies.
Make comparisons fair: compare products that meet the same need, on material, relevant, verifiable and representative features, and don't denigrate competitors or create confusion with their brands.
Make every ad recognisable as an ad: label advertorials, sponsored content and paid influencer posts clearly and prominently, where people will notice the label straight away.

Disclose any connection between an endorser and the brand that the audience wouldn't expect, such as payment, free or discounted products, or a family, employment or business relationship, clearly and close to the endorsement.
Use only genuine endorsements and reviews that reflect the honest opinion and real experience of the person giving them; never write, buy or fake reviews, and don't hide or suppress negative ones.
Make environmental claims specific, accurate and backed by evidence, base them on the product's full life cycle, and don't hide significant harms or present as a benefit what the law requires anyway.

Don't use vague green claims such as "eco-friendly", "green" or "sustainable" unless you can prove them without qualification, and don't use environmental labels or symbols that suggest a certification or official approval you don't have.
Base climate claims on real reductions in emissions, and say clearly how much of a claim such as "carbon neutral" rests on offsetting.

Take special care with children: don't exploit their credulity, inexperience or loyalty, don't urge them directly to buy or to get their parents to buy, and don't market products restricted by age, such as alcohol, gambling and tobacco, to minors.

Don't target or exploit people made vulnerable by age, illness, disability, credulity or their circumstances, such as bereavement or losing a job, and judge your marketing by its likely effect on them, not only on the average consumer.
Don't play on fear or distress without a good reason, and don't use shocking claims or images just to get attention; where fear is justified, for example in a safety message, keep it in proportion.
Don't use high-pressure tactics, or techniques that take advantage of people's trust or limited understanding to push them into choices they wouldn't otherwise make.

Check before you share: stop, ask who is behind a claim and where they got it, read beyond the headline, and look for other trustworthy reports, especially when a post tells you what you want to hear.
Credit creators and respect their terms: don't post someone else's work as your own, follow the licence when there is one, such as a Creative Commons licence, and ask permission when there isn't.
Don't harass, threaten, bully or impersonate anyone online, and don't attack people for who they are, such as their religion, ethnicity, nationality, gender or other identity.
Don't join pile-ons against a person, and never publish someone's home address, workplace, phone number or other personal details to expose them (doxing).
When you see someone being abused online, report it, check in with the person targeted, and help them get support.
Never share, or threaten to share, intimate images of someone without their consent, and never make or share sexual deepfakes of real people.
Ask before you post photos, videos or personal details of other people, respect a no, and take special care with children, including your own.
Protect your accounts: use a strong, separate password for your email, turn on two-step verification and keep your devices and apps updated.

If you come across sexual images of children, don't save or send them to anyone, even to warn others: report the web address to the platform and to a hotline, such as the Internet Watch Foundation in the UK or another member of the INHOPE network.
Report harmful content to the platform, and call the police if someone is in immediate danger.

Act solely in the public interest: never use your office, its powers, public money, property or official information for your own benefit or that of your family, friends, party or business associates.
Decide impartially, on the merits and the best evidence: treat everyone fairly, give no undue preference to any person or group, and never discriminate.
Appoint and promote people, and award public contracts, on merit through fair and open competition with objective criteria set in advance, and keep out favouritism and nepotism.
If you are a non-elected official, serve the lawful government of the day impartially, whatever its politics and your own, and don't let your office be used for party political purposes.

Declare your private interests, and deal with any conflict of interest before it affects your work: watch for conflicts, disclose them as soon as you are aware of them, and step back from decisions where your interests, or those of your family or associates, could influence you or appear to.
Refuse gifts, hospitality and favours that could influence your judgement, or reasonably look as if they could, and report any bribe that is offered to you.

Respect cooling-off periods when you leave public office: for the period the rules set, don't act or lobby for anyone on matters you dealt with in office, and never use confidential information from your former job.
Be truthful: never give ministers, the legislature or the public information you know or believe to be false or misleading, and don't withhold information that should properly be released.

Be open about decisions and the reasons for them: publish information about how your body works and decides, and answer requests for information on time; withhold information only for clear and lawful reasons.
Accept scrutiny: answer for your decisions to the public and to the bodies that oversee you, such as audit institutions, ombudsmen, regulators and courts, and respond properly to their findings.
Report corruption and other wrongdoing through the proper channels, and make sure that colleagues who report in good faith and on reasonable grounds suffer no reprisal.
Lead by example: if you hold senior office, show these principles in your own conduct, treat others with respect, support integrity actively and challenge poor behaviour wherever it occurs.

Notice when a decision has an ethical side, even when it is presented as a business, technical or personal matter: ask whether it could harm someone, treat someone unfairly, or benefit some people at others' expense.
Get the facts before you judge: what you know, what you don't know, and what you are only assuming.
Identify everyone the decision affects, and hear from them where you can, especially people who are vulnerable or have no voice in the decision.
Look for more options than the first two that come to mind, including ones that meet competing duties at once.
Test your choice before you act: would you be comfortable explaining it to someone you respect, to the people it affects, or in public?
Carry out your decision with care for everyone it affects, and afterwards reflect on how it turned out, what you learned and whether anything needs putting right (`ACCT-4`).
Expect your judgement to lean in your own favour, and look hardest at conclusions that benefit you, your team or your organisation.
Treat your own excuses as warning signs: "it didn't really hurt anyone", "others have done worse", "my boss made me", "they deserved it", "if I hadn't, someone else would have".

Notice when the situation is steering your choice: an authority you want to please, what the people around you are doing, pressure from your organisation, or a role in which you apply standards you wouldn't apply at home.
Decide where your limits are before you reach them, because each small compromise makes the next one easier.
Don't let a record of good deeds, or confidence in your own character, excuse you from thinking a choice through.
Talk a difficult decision through with people you trust, including people who don't share your interest in the outcome or your point of view, but keep the decision your own.
When duties conflict and you can't meet them all, act on the weightier one, then explain yourself to the people you let down and make it up to them where you can.
Care for your children: provide for their needs, protect them, and guide them as their abilities grow, with their best interests as your basic concern.
Never use violence, threats, intimidation or coercive control against a partner, a child, an older relative or anyone else in your household, and never neglect someone who depends on you.
Respect your parents and other older relatives, treat them with dignity, and support them when they need help or care.
Share the work of bringing up children and caring for relatives fairly, so that it doesn't fall on one person, and in particular not on women by default.
Be loyal to your family and friends, but never let loyalty lead you to do wrong, cover up wrongdoing or harm others for them.
Be a good friend: care about your friends for their own sake, share in their joys and troubles, and help them when they need it.
Thank the people who help you, and look for ways to return or pass on their kindness.
Be willing to forgive, but don't confuse forgiving with excusing the wrong, or with going back to someone who may harm you again.
Be a considerate neighbour: treat the people who live around you with respect, and look out for those who are old, ill or alone.
Contribute to the common good of the communities you belong to, for example by volunteering your time and skills.
Take part in the public life of your community: stay informed, vote where you can, and take part in decisions that affect the people around you.
Get each participant's free and informed consent before they take part, and respect their right to refuse or to withdraw at any time without penalty.
Have the research approved by an independent research ethics committee before it starts, and keep the committee informed until it ends.
Do research only when its expected value outweighs the risks and burdens to participants, keep those risks as low as possible, and stop or change the study if the balance turns.
Choose participants for scientific reasons, not because they are easy to recruit, and give people in vulnerable situations specific protections instead of excluding them by default.
Protect participants' privacy and the confidentiality of their data and samples, and reuse them only with consent or with a research ethics committee's approval.

Make sure that participants harmed by the research get free treatment and fair compensation, and arrange before a clinical trial starts how participants who still need a treatment shown to be beneficial will get it afterwards.
Never fabricate, falsify or plagiarise, whether you are proposing, doing, reviewing or reporting research.
Register each clinical trial and other medical study with people in a public registry before the first participant enrols, and make all the results public, including negative and inconclusive ones.
List as authors everyone who meets the authorship criteria, and only them, and acknowledge everyone else who contributed.
Disclose financial and other interests that could affect, or seem to affect, your research, in proposals, ethics applications, publications, peer reviews and public statements.

Report suspected research misconduct to the body responsible for investigating it, and handle allegations fairly: protect whistleblowers who act in good faith, and presume the accused innocent until proven otherwise.

Use animals only when no method without animals can answer the research question, and apply the 3Rs: replace animals wherever possible, reduce their number to what a sound design needs, and refine housing, care and procedures to minimise pain, suffering and distress.
Treat every person as someone with equal dignity, never merely as a tool for your own purposes.
Respect people's right to make their own decisions about their own lives, even decisions you think unwise.
When someone finds it hard to decide, help them decide for themselves; if you must decide for them, follow their wishes, values and preferences as far as you can.
Listen to children, and give their views a weight that grows with their age and maturity.
Get a person's consent before you do something to their body, their belongings or their private life, and respect a refusal.
Make sure consent is real: the person understands what they are agreeing to, agrees freely without pressure or threats, and is able to decide.
Treat consent as specific and revocable: agreeing to one thing is not agreeing to another, agreeing once is not agreeing every time, and anyone can change their mind at any point.
Respect other people's privacy: don't read their messages, search their belongings, track them or record them in private without their agreement.
Keep what people tell you in confidence, and don't spread personal information or gossip that could hurt them.

Influence people only by honest means, such as reasons, evidence and sincere requests: don't coerce them with threats, and don't manipulate them with guilt trips, emotional blackmail, peer pressure, stoked-up fears or by making them doubt their own judgement.
Before you override someone's choice for their own good, make sure they know the risks and are able to decide; warn, inform and offer help rather than force, and intervene only as far as needed.
Never torture anyone or treat them in a cruel, inhuman or degrading way, and never take part in it, whatever the order, threat or emergency.
Never hold anyone in slavery or servitude, or make them do forced labour, and never knowingly profit from it.
Never take part in, incite or help genocide: acts intended to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.
Respect everyone's freedom of thought, conscience and religion, including their freedom to change their religion or belief, and never coerce anyone into or out of a belief.
Never stir up hatred against people because of their nationality, race or religion in a way that incites discrimination, hostility or violence.
Respect other people's freedom to hold and express opinions, including ones you reject, and answer speech you disagree with by argument, not by threats, violence or intimidation.
In every decision that affects a child, make the child's best interests a primary consideration.
Use your own rights and freedoms in ways that respect the rights of others.
Refuse to take part in violating anyone's human rights, by what you do or by failing to act where you must, even when you are ordered or pressured to.
Don't knowingly help others abuse human rights, by supplying, financing, encouraging or covering up for them, and don't knowingly profit from their abuses.
Stand up, by peaceful means, for the rights of others, especially people who can't easily defend themselves.

If you run or manage an organisation, make sure it respects human rights: commit to it in a policy, find out what harm its activities and business relationships cause or contribute to, prevent it, and put right what it causes.
Test only systems you own, have permission to test, or that the owner has opened to research in a published vulnerability disclosure policy, and stay within its scope and terms.
Do only what you need to show that a vulnerability exists: don't disrupt services, change or destroy data, or harm the experience of users.

If a vulnerability gives you access to personal or confidential data, access only the minimum needed to prove it, stop testing and report it straight away; use only test accounts you own or have permission to use.

Get ethics review for research that collects data about people or could affect systems at scale, such as internet-wide measurements, and weigh the risks to third parties who never agreed to take part.
Report a vulnerability first to the vendor or owner through its official channel, or through a coordinator such as a national CERT if you can't reach it or it doesn't respond.
Agree a disclosure date with the vendor, give it a reasonable time to fix the problem before you publish, and publish once a fix is available or the agreed deadline has passed.

Move faster when a vulnerability is being exploited or threatens critical infrastructure, health or safety: involve a coordinator, and shorten the disclosure timeline so that people can protect themselves.
When you publish, give users and defenders enough detail to judge their risk and protect themselves, and weigh what extra detail, such as a working exploit, would give attackers.
When a vulnerability affects several vendors or a shared component, coordinate with all of them, directly or through a coordinator, so that users of every affected product can be protected.
Never use a vulnerability to threaten its owner or demand payment, and don't make your report or your silence depend on a reward.
If you receive vulnerability reports, make reporting easy, presume the reporter acts in good faith, respond promptly, keep them informed and don't take legal action against good-faith research.
Put the health, safety and welfare of the public first: when what a client, employer or user wants conflicts with it, the public comes first.
Before you build or change a system, work out who it could affect and how, including people who aren't its users and those with the least power, and look again as it changes.

Raise concerns about software that could cause harm with the people responsible, take them to an appropriate authority if they don't act, and refuse to take part in work you believe breaks your profession's code.
Be honest about what software can and can't do: describe its capabilities, limits, risks and test results accurately, and don't make claims you can't support.
Give realistic estimates of cost, time and quality, with their uncertainty, and tell your client or employer early if a project is likely to fail, overrun or cause other problems.
Take on only work you are competent to do, or say plainly what you lack, and keep your knowledge up to date.
Own your mistakes: find, fix and report errors in your work, and seek and accept honest review of it.
Use code, data, models and tools only as their licences and owners allow, and credit the people whose work you build on.

Approve or release software only when you have good grounds to believe it is safe and adequately tested, and take special care with systems that people's lives, health or essential services depend on.
Build security and privacy in from the start: model the threats, collect and keep only the personal data the software needs, and make secure settings the default.
Make software accessible to people with disabilities, following WCAG for web content, and think about who else it could exclude, for example through cost or the devices it needs.

Look at an important decision through several theories, not only the one that comes most naturally to you: what it does to the wellbeing of everyone affected, which duties and rights are at stake, what it shows about your character, what the relationships involved need, and whether you could justify it to each person affected.
Treat agreement between the theories as a reason for confidence, and disagreement as a reason to look harder before you act.
Be wary of reaching for whichever theory justifies what you already wanted to do.
Use the theories to inform your judgement, not to replace it.
Test general principles against your considered judgements about clear cases, and those judgements against the principles, and revise whichever gives way.
Before you act, ask whether you would accept the action if you were in the other person's place, and whether you could justify it to everyone it affects.
Never use forced or child labour, including work that is exacted under threat of a penalty or not freely chosen, and debt bondage.

Recruit, pay, train, promote and dismiss people on the basis of their ability to do the job, never because of race, colour, sex, religion, political opinion, national extraction or social origin, or other grounds that the law protects where you work, such as age, disability or sexual orientation.

Pay women and men equally for work of equal value, not only for the same work: compare jobs on objective factors, such as the qualifications, effort and responsibility they need and the conditions they are done in, not on who usually does them.

Recruit fairly: don't charge workers or jobseekers any recruitment fees or related costs, give them clear terms they can understand, preferably in a written contract, and never confiscate or keep their identity documents.
Pay fair wages that allow a decent life, and respect reasonable limits on working hours, rest and paid holidays.

Make work safe and healthy: keep workplaces, machinery, equipment and processes safe so far as reasonably practicable, consult workers on safety, don't make them pay for safety measures, and never penalise someone for leaving a situation they reasonably believe is an imminent and serious danger.

Don't harass anyone and don't tolerate violence or harassment at work, including sexual and other gender-based harassment: adopt a policy with your workers, assess the risks, train people, and offer safe, fair ways to complain.
Respect workers' freedom to form and join trade unions and to bargain collectively, and never refuse to hire, dismiss or otherwise punish anyone for union membership or activities.

Never retaliate against anyone who raises a concern in good faith about wrongdoing, danger or harassment, whether they raise it inside the organisation or with a regulator, and protect their identity.
Give people safe ways to raise concerns in confidence, and anonymously if they wish; investigate what they report independently and in proportion, and act on it.
Lead by example: if you lead others, act with integrity yourself, show in your own conduct the behaviour you ask of them, and promote a culture of integrity.
Give credit for work to the people who did it, in reports, presentations and appraisals, and don't present a colleague's or a team member's work as your own.
